blocks.prompt: The Bug That Pretends to Be a Twig
blocks.text: A stick insect does not run away. It does not bite. It hides in plain sight. Its long brown body looks like a twig. Its legs look like little branches. When a bird looks right at it, the bird sees a stick and flies on. If the wind blows the leaves, the stick insect rocks back and forth. Now it looks like a twig moving in the wind. Stick insects eat leaves. They eat at night when it is dark and safe. A young stick insect hatches from an egg that looks like a tiny seed. It is already a tiny stick.

blocks.prompt: Doing Nothing, Very Well
blocks.text:
A stick insect spends its whole life pretending to be something boring. Its body is long and thin and brown, shaped exactly like a twig. Its legs look like small side branches. Some kinds even have bumps that look like buds, or notches that look like the spot where a leaf fell off.

Hiding is only half the job. The insect also has to act like a twig. So it stays still for hours. When a breeze moves the leaves around it, the stick insect rocks gently back and forth, as if the wind were pushing it too. A twig that sways with the wind looks like a twig. A twig that walks looks like lunch.

If a bird grabs a stick insect by the leg, the insect can let that leg go and escape. Later, when it molts and climbs out of its old skin, a new leg grows in. The new leg is often a little smaller than the old one.

Stick insects eat leaves, mostly at night. In the dark they do not need to hide as carefully, and there are fewer birds watching.

notes: Order Phasmatodea, from a Greek word for phantom
Eggs look like seeds and fool ants

The longest insects on Earth

blocks.prompt: The Egg That Ants Carry Home
blocks.text:
Almost everything about a stick insect is a disguise, including its eggs.

A female stick insect does not build a nest. She drops her eggs one at a time from wherever she happens to be standing, and they fall to the forest floor like a slow rain of seeds. That comparison is not an accident. Stick insect eggs are hard, oval, and patterned, and they look remarkably like plant seeds. Many of them carry a small fatty knob on one end called a capitulum. Ants love it. An ant finds the egg, decides it has found a seed, and hauls it back to the nest. Underground, the ants chew off the fatty knob and leave the rest of the egg alone. The egg is now buried, safe from birds and from fire, inside an ant nest. Months later a young stick insect hatches and climbs out.

Some plants use ants in exactly the same way to move their seeds. The stick insect copies the trick.

There is a stranger detail. In many species a female can lay eggs that hatch with no male involved at all. The young are copies of their mother, and they are all female. Scientists call this parthenogenesis. It means a single stick insect, alone on a single bush, can start a whole population.

Stick insects are also the longest insects on Earth. The record holders live in Southeast Asia and stretch more than 60 centimeters with their legs held out, which is longer than your arm.

notes: Dryococelus australis: the Lord Howe Island stick insect

blocks.prompt: The Insect That Came Back
blocks.text:
Lord Howe Island sits in the Tasman Sea, off the east coast of Australia. It once swarmed with a stick insect so large and glossy that people called it the tree lobster. Dryococelus australis grew as long as a human hand, could not fly, and was common enough that fishermen used it as bait.

In 1918 a supply ship called the Makambo ran aground at the island. Black rats came ashore with the cargo. Within about two years the tree lobster was gone. By the middle of the century it was written off as extinct, which is the ordinary ending for this kind of story.

This one did not end there. About twenty kilometers away stands Ball's Pyramid, a blade of bare rock rising straight out of the ocean, too steep for almost anything to live on. Climbers in the 1960s found a few dead stick insects there, which was tantalizing but proved nothing. In 2001 two Australian scientists, David Priddel and Nicholas Carlile, climbed the spire at night with flashlights. Partway up, on a narrow ledge, they found a single melaleuca shrub. Under it lived about twenty four tree lobsters. That was the entire species.

In 2003 researchers took two breeding pairs off the rock. One female, nicknamed Eve, nearly died and was nursed through the night by a keeper with a mixture that included calcium. She survived, and she laid. Melbourne Zoo has since raised thousands of her descendants. In 2019 Lord Howe Island ran a program to remove its rats, clearing the way for the tree lobster to come home.

It is worth being honest about the odds. A species rebuilt from a handful of animals carries very little genetic variety, and an island is a fragile place to bet on. But the arithmetic is still remarkable. Twenty four insects, one bush, one ledge, on a rock in the open sea. That is how close it came.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Phasmatodea, from the Greek phasma, a phantom
Masquerade: seen, and dismissed as a twig
Some species have gone millions of years with no males
Eggs can survive passing through a bird
Longest insects on Earth, past 60 centimeters
About 3,000 known species worldwide

blocks.prompt: The Phantom Order: What a Stick Insect Is Actually Doing
blocks.text:
Entomologists file stick insects under the order Phasmatodea, built from the Greek word phasma, meaning phantom. It is an unusually good piece of naming, because the animal's entire strategy is to be present and unnoticed.

It is worth separating two ideas that get blurred together. Camouflage asks not to be seen. A moth on matching bark is camouflaged: the predator's eye passes over it without registering anything. Masquerade is different and stranger. A masquerading animal is seen perfectly well, and then dismissed. The bird looks straight at the stick insect, registers a twig, files it under things that are not food, and moves on. The insect wins not by disappearing but by being correctly identified as something worthless. This is why the details matter so much. Bumps that read as buds, a kink in the body that reads as a broken branch, legs held tight against the body in a line: each one is not hiding the animal, it is arguing a case. And the argument must survive scrutiny, which is why so many species rock gently on the spot. A rigid twig in a moving canopy is a wrong note.

The reproductive strategy is where things get genuinely peculiar. Many phasmids reproduce by parthenogenesis: a female lays unfertilized eggs that hatch into daughters genetically identical to her. In several lineages males are rare, and in some they appear to have been absent for a very long time. The advantage is obvious. One female blown onto an empty island can found a population by herself, and every individual she produces is a reproducing female rather than a male who cannot lay. The cost is equally obvious, and it is the reason sex persists across most of life. Clones cannot shuffle their genes. A population without variation meets a new disease or a new climate with a single answer, and if that answer is wrong, everyone is wrong at once. Evolution rewards whatever survives the next season, not whatever is wisest in the long run.

Even the eggs are strategic. They are hard, seed shaped, and often tipped with a fatty capitulum that attracts ants, which carry the eggs into their nests, eat the knob, and unknowingly bury the rest somewhere safe from birds and fire. Researchers have gone further and tested whether phasmid eggs can survive being eaten by a bird outright. In feeding trials, a small fraction passed through the gut intact and later hatched. If that happens in the wild, it would give a flightless insect a way to cross water it could never walk across, carried in the one place it would seem least likely to survive.

What holds all of this together is a single constraint. The stick insect is slow, soft, and mostly defenseless. It cannot outrun a bird, it cannot fight one, and in many species it cannot fly away. Everything it has instead is an answer to that fact: the shape, the stillness, the swaying, the seed shaped egg, the female who needs no mate. The order is well named. A phantom is not something that isn't there. It is something that is there, and that you have decided to explain away.
